ambiguities.evidence: Theorem 1.3.1 lists only 'i.i.d. random variables with mean µ'; Section 1.1 identifies mean with the Lebesgue-integral expectation.
ambiguities.impact: A formalization will normally expose integrability as an explicit hypothesis or typeclass condition, even though the source packages it into the phrase 'with mean µ'.
ambiguities.issue: The theorem says 'with mean µ' rather than explicitly stating an absolute-integrability condition.

contract_plain_english: If X₁, X₂, ... are independent and identically distributed real random variables with common finite mean µ, then their sample averages (X₁ + ··· + X_N)/N converge to µ almost surely; no finite-variance assumption is required.

source_evidence.anchor: Theorem 1.3.1 (Strong law of large numbers). Let X1, X2, ... be a sequence of i.i.d. random variables with mean µ
source_evidence.location: PDF page 5; printed page 9; Theorem 1.3.1 heading and first sentence
source_evidence.observation: The theorem binds an infinite i.i.d. sequence with common mean µ and states no variance hypothesis.

source_evidence.anchor: Consider the sum SN = X1 + · · · + XN
source_evidence.observation: S_N is the partial sum of the first N variables.

source_evidence.anchor: Then, as N → ∞, SN/N → µ almost surely
source_evidence.location: PDF page 5; printed page 9; conclusion of Theorem 1.3.1
source_evidence.observation: The normalized partial sums converge to µ in the almost-sure mode.

binders: An infinite sequence X₁, X₂, ... of real-valued random variables on a common probability space.
For each positive integer N, the partial sum S_N.
conclusions: As N → ∞, S_N/N converges to µ almost surely.
definitions_and_conventions: i.i.d. means independent and identically distributed.
Almost-sure convergence means that S_N(ω)/N converges to µ for all ω in an event of probability one.
hypotheses: The sequence is independent and identically distributed.
The random variables have mean µ, hence the common expectation is finite in the ordinary real-valued sense.
implicit_context: All Xᵢ are defined on the same probability space.
N tends to infinity through positive integers.
The scalar µ is viewed as the corresponding constant random variable when expressing almost-sure convergence.
The phrase 'with mean µ' supplies the integrability needed for the strong law; finite variance is not assumed.

details: The theorem concerns one infinite i.i.d. sequence and its successive partial sums.
The partial sum S_N is divided by N, producing the sample mean.
The conclusion is almost-sure convergence, not merely convergence in probability, in distribution, or of expectations.
A common finite mean is assumed.
No finite-variance hypothesis appears in Theorem 1.3.1.
The limit is the common mean µ.

undebatable_constraints: The family is an infinite i.i.d. sequence.
The variables have common mean µ.
S_N is the sum of the first N variables.
The normalized quantity is exactly S_N/N.
The convergence mode is almost sure.
The theorem does not assume finite variance.
